newsitem.title: USA: Hard to say how much US economy slowing--Broaddus.
newsitem.headline: Hard to say how much US economy slowing--Broaddus.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Alfred Broaddus said on Wednesday it was unclear the extent to which the economy was cooling down after a spurt of growth in the fourth quarter of last year.

"It's hard to say," Broaddus said in response to a question from a reporter about whether the economy appeared as though it was slowing toward the two percent or slighlty above growth rate that the Fed considers sustainable.
Broaddus noted that the Fed's central tendency forecast for gross domestic product growth overall in 1997 was two to 2.25 percent.
The economy grew by 3.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Concerning the outlook for the economy, Broaddus said, "My own feeling is there is certainly some upside risk."
Broaddus, who spoke with reporters after moderating a panel at a National Association of Business Economists conference, added, "most labor markets appear reasonably tight."

Asked about the extent to which the concept of a non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) figures into his judgements of the inflation outlook, Broaddus said the NAIRU fluctuates a great deal, which makes it difficult to rely on.
"It gives me some pause in placing undue weight on it," he said.

Broaddus was also questioned about the extent to which the Fed is looking at Labor Department statistics on job leavers to gauge the extent of the perceived worker insecurity that may have helped hold down wage demands.
He replied, "It's a piece of information that we can tuck in with all the others. I don't think you can draw any firm conclusions from it."
